title: Prediction bias in biological ageing models
summary: Biological ageing markers have attracted growing interest, with models estimating age from organ imaging or blood biomarkers. An estimated age above chronological age or the age-specific population expectation is assumed to reflect accelerated ageing and poorer health. Previous research has supported this assumption through positive associations between disease and age gaps or acceleration. However, in this study, we identified a widespread health-dependent prediction bias in ageing markers that affects their key interpretation and application. Specifically, we investigated five ageing markers derived from retinal images, brain MRI, chest radiographs, abdominal CT, and blood tests, and evaluated them using association analyses. We observed the well-recognised phenomenon of regression to the mean (RTM) in the four organ-image based markers, whereby estimated ages were shifted towards the mean age of the training cohort. More importantly, we revealed that the strength of RTM varied with health status, with stronger RTM in unhealthy than in healthy individuals. This differential RTM introduced a health-dependent prediction bias that persisted after calibration and systematically altered associations across age subgroups, suggesting that whole cohort associations may not reflect those observed within individual age subgroups. Additionally, we showed that the tested ageing markers, including PhenoAge derived from blood biomarkers, had limited ability to distinguish health status at the individual level. These findings call for careful interpretation of biological ageing markers and their use in clinical studies, and highlight the need for further development and validation before these ageing markers can reliably inform individual health assessments.

AI.tldr: This study reveals a widespread health-dependent prediction bias in biological ageing markers, driven by differential regression to the mean, which distorts key interpretations and applications of these markers.
AI.motivation: Biological ageing markers assume that an estimated age above chronological age reflects accelerated ageing and poorer health, an assumption supported by positive disease-age gap associations. This study questions whether that assumption holds given the statistical behavior of these models.
AI.method: They investigated five ageing markers derived from retinal images, brain MRI, chest radiographs, abdominal CT, and blood tests, evaluating them via association analyses.
AI.result: Regression to the mean (RTM) was observed in the four organ-image markers, shifting estimated ages toward the training cohort mean. RTM strength varied with health status (stronger in unhealthy individuals), producing a health-dependent prediction bias that persisted after calibration and altered associations across age subgroups. The markers, including PhenoAge, showed limited individual-level ability to distinguish health status.
AI.conclusion: Biological ageing markers require careful interpretation and their use in clinical studies should be cautious; further development and validation are needed before they can reliably inform individual health assessments.

title: Prevalence and the rate of antigenic evolution are jointly determined in an eco-evolutionary SIR model
summary: Influenza A persists by continually changing the antigens that its host population recognizes. How fast it evolves and how many hosts it infects are not independent, because the immunity that selects new variants is produced by the infections the pathogen has already caused. We analyze a model of Andreasen et.\ al.\ that captures this eco-evolutionary feedback, and we extend it to the case where infection may kill the host. In the model infected and recovered hosts are distributions over a one-dimensional antigenic space coupled by cross-immunity. The endemic state is a traveling pulse: the infected distribution keeps a fixed shape and advances through antigenic space at constant speed. In the limit of weak antigenic mutation we construct the pulse asymptotically and find that: (i) the speed of antigenic evolution decreases as prevalence rises, (ii) less standing antigenic variation accompanies either faster or slower antigenic evolution, depending on whether pathogens differ in immune evasion or host lifespan (iii) the total number of infected hosts is largest at an intermediate virulence when the host birth rate is sufficiently low.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Andreasen et al.'s model of influenza A eco-evolutionary dynamics to include infection-induced host mortality, constructing the endemic traveling-pulse solution asymptotically in the weak-mutation limit.
AI.motivation: Influenza A's antigenic evolution and infection prevalence are coupled: immunity that selects new variants arises from past infections. Understanding this feedback, and how virulence (host killing) alters it, requires a tractable model of the endemic state.
AI.method: The authors analyze a model where infected and recovered hosts are distributions over a 1D antigenic space linked by cross-immunity, extending it to allow infection-caused host death. The endemic state is a traveling pulse (fixed shape, constant speed through antigenic space); they construct this pulse asymptotically in the weak-antigenic-mutation limit.
AI.result: (i) Antigenic evolution speed decreases as prevalence rises. (ii) Less standing antigenic variation accompanies either faster or slower evolution, depending on whether pathogens differ in immune evasion or host lifespan. (iii) Total infected hosts is largest at intermediate virulence when host birth rate is sufficiently low.
AI.conclusion: The eco-evolutionary feedback produces a traveling-pulse endemic state whose properties link evolutionary speed, antigenic diversity, prevalence, and virulence in non-trivial ways, with virulence maximizing total infections at intermediate levels under low host birth rates.

title: Pathways of early evolution from the perspectives of a riboreplisome -- the ultimate RNA machine of life
summary: Translation of the genetic code into proteins is universal across life, with ribosomes serving as the ancient molecular machines enabling this information transformation. We propose that early replication and protein biosynthesis were inseparable functions performed by a single ancient RNA molecule: the riboreplisome. This hypothesis addresses fundamental challenges facing RNA world, protein world, and RNA-protein co-evolution theories -- particularly the problem of non-Darwinian starting points and the interdependence of replication and translation machineries. We present a 12-step evolutionary pathway from simple RNA replicase to proto-ribosome, supported by quantitative modelling demonstrating that only two steps require non-Darwinian transitions while the remaining ten proceed through standard selection. The single-molecule riboreplisome architecture provides an approximately 6-fold evolutionary advantage over multi-component "RNA soup" scenarios, principally by maintaining genetic linkage and retaining catalytic products close to the replicating genome (resisting diffusion loss); structural resistance to parasitic "cheater" molecules follows as a corollary. The riboreplisome framework explains the origins of ribosomal, transfer, and messenger RNA as derivatives of a single ancestral molecule, while providing a driving force for cellular compartmentalisation. Although the original riboreplisome is likely lost to deep time, molecular remnants may persist in extant biological RNA. Identification or reconstruction of riboreplisome-like molecules could advance both origin-of-life research and synthetic biology applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the "riboreplisome," a single ancient RNA molecule that combined replication and protein biosynthesis, arguing this resolves key problems in origin-of-life theories via a 12-step evolutionary pathway requiring only two non-Darwinian transitions.
AI.motivation: RNA world, protein world, and co-evolution theories all face fundamental challenges, notably non-Darwinian starting points and the interdependence of replication and translation machineries. The authors seek a unified framework that explains how these functions could have originated together.
AI.method: The authors propose a conceptual hypothesis of a single-molecule "riboreplisome" and develop a 12-step evolutionary pathway from simple RNA replicase to proto-ribosome. They support it with quantitative modelling comparing single-molecule versus multi-component "RNA soup" scenarios.
AI.result: Only two of the 12 steps require non-Darwinian transitions, with the remaining ten proceeding via standard selection. The single-molecule architecture offers ~6-fold evolutionary advantage over multi-component scenarios by maintaining genetic linkage and retaining catalytic products near the replicating genome (resisting diffusion loss). Resistance to parasitic "cheaters" follows as a corollary.
AI.conclusion: The riboreplisome framework explains the origins of ribosomal, transfer, and messenger RNA as derivatives of a single ancestral molecule and provides a driving force for cellular compartmentalisation. Though the original molecule is likely lost to deep time, remnants may persist in extant RNA; identification or reconstruction could advance origin-of-life research and synthetic biology.

title: Large-deviations theory for growing chemical reaction networks
summary: Growing biochemical systems are intrinsically noisy, with one important source of stochasticity arising from the discrete reaction events of the underlying biochemical network. Because growing systems do not generally admit stationary abundance distributions, it is unclear how to separate this intrinsic chemical noise from other sources of variability in population and single-cell data. Here we develop a large-deviation theory for exponentially growing stochastic chemical reaction networks by decomposing abundance into volume and composition. In these coordinates, balanced growth corresponds to a stable composition together with exponentially increasing volume. We show that composition fluctuations satisfy a large-deviation principle with speed equal to the volume of the growing system, and the corresponding quasipotential is selected by a solution of the contact Hamilton--Jacobi equation. We also derive a fluctuation theory for accumulated observables and show that their covariances decay with accumulated-volume, rather than with physical time. Applications to a minimal autocatalytic network and a coarse-grained cellular growth model demonstrate how the theory predicts composition quasipotentials, growth-rate fluctuations, and correlations between observables. The framework therefore provides a stochastic null model for single-cell heterogeneity generated by the intrinsic stochasticity of the underlying chemical reaction network.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a large-deviation theory for exponentially growing stochastic chemical reaction networks, separating intrinsic chemical noise from other variability by decomposing abundance into volume and composition.
AI.motivation: Growing biochemical systems are intrinsically noisy due to discrete reaction events. Since growing systems lack stationary abundance distributions, it is unclear how to separate intrinsic chemical noise from other variability in population and single-cell data.
AI.method: The authors decompose abundance into volume and composition, where balanced growth corresponds to stable composition with exponentially increasing volume. They establish a large-deviation principle for composition fluctuations with speed equal to system volume, with the quasipotential determined by the contact Hamilton-Jacobi equation. They also derive a fluctuation theory for accumulated observables.
AI.result: Composition fluctuations satisfy a large-deviation principle with speed equal to growing-system volume. Accumulated observable covariances decay with accumulated volume rather than physical time. Applications to a minimal autocatalytic network and a coarse-grained cellular growth model predict composition quasipotentials, growth-rate fluctuations, and correlations between observables.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a stochastic null model for single-cell heterogeneity arising from intrinsic stochasticity of the underlying chemical reaction network.

title: Predicting Mutational Signature Exposures from H&E Whole Slide Images: A Pan-Cancer Feasibility Study
summary: Mutational signatures reveal cancer-driving processes with clinical relevance: MMR-deficient tumors respond better to immunotherapy, HRD tumors are sensitive to PARP inhibitors, and POLE-mutant tumors often have high mutation burdens influencing treatment response. Yet signature profiling remains limited by the cost, complexity, and turnaround time of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) or whole-exome sequencing. Histopathology is widely available and cost-effective, and H&E morphology has been linked to MSI, HRD, POLE-related processes, and driver mutations. Whether histology can recover the broader landscape of mutational signature exposures in a pan-cancer setting remains unknown. Here we introduce Hist2Sig, a deep learning framework predicting exposures to 30 COSMIC SBS signatures from H&E-stained slides. Trained on matched WGS and histology data from 7,063 TCGA patients across 29 cancer types, Hist2Sig was compared with a tumor type-only baseline to separate morphology-derived signal from tissue-of-origin priors. In internal cross-validation, it recovered relative signature compositions across most tumor types and achieved higher mean top-three overlap than the baseline in 19 of 29, with the largest gains in COAD, PRAD, GBM, and UCEC. It also recurrently recovered signatures of poorly characterized etiology, including SBS8, SBS12, SBS39, and SBS40a. In an external CPTAC cohort of 193 patients across five tumor types, Hist2Sig retained moderate concordance with observed compositions and outperformed the baseline in glioblastoma and pancreatic adenocarcinoma. These results support the feasibility of inferring mutational signature exposures from routine histology, while highlighting variation across tumor types. Hist2Sig provides a foundation for tumor-specific models that could complement sequencing in pre-sequencing triage or support decisions where WGS is unavailable.

AI.tldr: Hist2Sig predicts 30 COSMIC SBS mutational signature exposures directly from H&E-stained histopathology slides, showing morphology carries recoverable mutational-signature information across cancer types.
AI.motivation: Mutational signatures have clinical value (MMR-deficiency predicting immunotherapy response, HRD sensitivity to PARP inhibitors, POLE-mutant high mutation burden), but profiling them requires costly, complex, slow WGS/WES. Histopathology is cheap and widely available, and H&E morphology has been linked to specific alterations like MSI, HRD, and POLE, but whether histology can recover the broader pan-cancer mutational signature landscape was unknown.
AI.method: Hist2Sig is a deep learning framework trained on matched WGS and histology data from 7,063 TCGA patients across 29 cancer types to predict exposures to 30 COSMIC SBS signatures from H&E slides. A tumor-type-only baseline was used to separate morphology-derived signal from tissue-of-origin priors. Evaluation included internal cross-validation and external validation on 193 CPTAC patients across five tumor types.
AI.result: In internal cross-validation, Hist2Sig recovered relative signature compositions across most tumor types and achieved higher mean top-three overlap than baseline in 19 of 29 types, with largest gains in COAD, PRAD, GBM, and UCEC. It recurrently recovered poorly characterized signatures (SBS8, SBS12, SBS39, SBS40a). Externally in CPTAC, it retained moderate concordance and beat baseline in glioblastoma and pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
AI.conclusion: Inferring mutational signature exposures from routine histology is feasible, though performance varies across tumor types. Hist2Sig provides a foundation for tumor-specific models that could complement sequencing in pre-sequencing triage or support decisions where WGS is unavailable.

title: Grid-cell firing fields lack local sixfold symmetry
summary: The firing fields of a grid cell form a hexagonal lattice, yet each field's intrinsic geometric structure remains unclear: Are individual grid fields radially symmetric or do they exhibit (weak) sixfold modulation inherited from the global lattice? To address this question, we quantified the within-field angular structure using harmonic analysis and per-cell matched simulations that preserved sampling statistics, field scale, and lattice geometry after correction for global elliptic deformation. We found that, across the investigated cells, the sixfold harmonic power fraction was consistent with values from matched locally circular reference fields. Experimental fields further showed substantially less sixfold modulation than matched simulations with an imposed local sixfold component, demonstrating sensitivity to sixfold structure at that level. This conclusion was supported by a complementary sixfold regression metric, harmonic leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, and robustness checks across radial-window choices, smoothing, and simulated background-noise levels. An observation-matched Burak--Fiete continuous-attractor network likewise showed no selective local sixfold enhancement despite its globally periodic grid structure, and this conclusion persisted when grid scale and relative field width were matched more closely to the experimental regime. These results suggest that the global hexagonal lattice organization need not be accompanied by detectable local sixfold angular modulation of individual firing fields, placing quantitative constraints on grid-field microstructure and mechanistic models of grid formation.

AI.tldr: Individual grid-cell firing fields are locally circular/radially symmetric, showing no detectable sixfold angular modulation despite the global hexagonal lattice organization.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear whether individual grid fields are radially symmetric or inherit weak sixfold modulation from the global hexagonal lattice. Resolving this constrains grid-field microstructure and models of grid formation.
AI.method: Harmonic analysis of within-field angular structure, using per-cell matched simulations preserving sampling statistics, field scale, and lattice geometry after correcting for global elliptic deformation. Supported by a sixfold regression metric, harmonic leave-one-out sensitivity, robustness checks (radial window, smoothing, noise), and an observation-matched Burak--Fiete continuous-attractor network.
AI.result: Experimental sixfold harmonic power fractions matched locally circular reference fields and were far below simulations with imposed local sixfold modulation. The Burak--Fiete network showed no selective local sixfold enhancement even when scale and relative field width were matched.
AI.conclusion: Global hexagonal lattice organization need not produce detectable local sixfold angular modulation of individual fields, placing quantitative constraints on grid-field microstructure and mechanistic models of grid formation.

title: Learning a non-linguistic code for inferred rules from reward
summary: How can a rule inferred from examples reach someone who never saw them, without a shared code? Patients with severe aphasia do it by gesture or sketch. One network sees worked examples and emits eight invented symbols; a second, blind to them, applies them to a new input. Rewarded for the second's success, the first learns a code carrying rules to three-step transformations training never presents, which new learners acquire. Like invented human languages, the code has two regimes: under reward alone the speaker drifts to one message, as human languages lose words under plain transmission; expressive pressure keeps messages differentiated. Success on new rules tracks how much the message says about the rule, not how varied messages are. The learning signal shapes the code: reward sorts many rules under few fixed labels; the listener's error gradient gives each rule a region of similar messages, telling rules apart far better.

AI.tldr: Two neural networks develop a shared symbolic code that transmits inferable rules to naive learners, even generalizing to unseen three-step transformations, analogous to how aphasia patients communicate via gesture without shared code.
AI.motivation: Investigate how a rule learned from examples can be conveyed to someone who never saw those examples, without any pre-existing shared code—as severe aphasia patients do via gesture/sketch.
AI.method: A speaker network sees worked examples and emits eight invented symbols; a listener network, blind to the examples, applies the symbols to a new input. The speaker is rewarded for listener success and learns a code; new learners then acquire it.
AI.result: The code carries rules for three-step transformations never seen in training and is learnable by new learners. It shows two regimes: reward alone collapses to one message (like human language word loss), while expressive pressure maintains differentiation. Generalization tracks rule-relevance of messages, not message diversity.
AI.conclusion: The learning signal shapes the code: reward sorts many rules under few fixed labels, whereas the listener's error gradient assigns each rule a region of similar messages, far better at distinguishing rules.

title: SatoyamaCT: A Multi-Axis Night-IR Camera-Trap Benchmark for Monitoring Crop-Damaging Wildlife in Japanese Agroforestry
summary: Crop and forest damage from sika deer, wild boar, and Japanese macaque is a serious economic problem in Japanese satoyama, where farmland and forest intermingle. Camera traps enable scalable monitoring, yet existing benchmarks evaluate recognition in-distribution, rarely prioritize night infrared imagery, and do not jointly address regional domain shift, novel-species detection, and uncertainty-based triage on a single dataset. We introduce the Satoyama Camera Trap Dataset (SatoyamaCT), 12,642 expert-verified crops from night-IR-dominant camera traps across three satoyama regions. An iterative annotation protocol combining BioCLIP embeddings with confidence-ordered confirmation reduced expert effort while all labels were verified by domain ecologists; species-level inter-annotator agreement reached Cohen's kappa = 0.900. A multi-axis protocol jointly evaluates domain generalization across region, camera placement, and illumination; open-set novel-species detection; and selective prediction, all under capture-event-based leakage control. Difficulty separates into distinct failure modes: a data-inherent regional gap of 16 to 27 percentage points persists in Wakayama across four backbones and domain-generalization methods including CORAL, DANN, and GroupDRO, and open-set detection reaches AUROC 0.93 to 0.96 overall yet degrades jointly with classification in Wakayama. Selective prediction recovers Wakayama accuracy from 0.593 to 0.815 at 50% coverage, supporting an uncertainty-aware triage workflow for practical pest monitoring in agroforestry.

AI.tldr: SatoyamaCT is a new expert-verified camera-trap benchmark (12,642 night-IR-dominant crops, 3 regions) with a multi-axis protocol evaluating regional domain shift, open-set novel-species detection, and selective prediction, revealing a persistent 16-27pp Wakayama gap and recovering accuracy to 0.815 at 50% coverage.
AI.motivation: Crop and forest damage by sika deer, wild boar, and Japanese macaque is a serious economic problem in Japanese satoyama. Camera traps enable scalable monitoring, but existing benchmarks evaluate in-distribution recognition, rarely prioritize night infrared imagery, and fail to jointly address regional domain shift, novel-species detection, and uncertainty-based triage on a single dataset.
AI.method: The authors introduce SatoyamaCT, with 12,642 expert-verified crops from night-IR-dominant traps across three satoyama regions. An iterative annotation protocol combines BioCLIP embeddings with confidence-ordered confirmation, all labels verified by domain ecologists (species-level Cohen's kappa = 0.900). A multi-axis protocol jointly evaluates domain generalization (region, camera placement, illumination), open-set novel-species detection, and selective prediction, under capture-event-based leakage control.
AI.result: A data-inherent regional gap of 16-27 percentage points persists in Wakayama across four backbones and domain-generalization methods (CORAL, DANN, GroupDRO). Open-set detection reaches AUROC 0.93-0.96 overall but degrades jointly with classification in Wakayama. Selective prediction recovers Wakayama accuracy from 0.593 to 0.815 at 50% coverage.
AI.conclusion: SatoyamaCT provides a realistic, multi-axis benchmark for camera-trap recognition, exposing distinct failure modes and supporting an uncertainty-aware triage workflow for practical pest monitoring in agroforestry.

title: Improving Molecular-Morphology Contrastive Pretraining using Deep-Learning-based Morphology Profiles
summary: Recent advancements in image-based profiling techniques have enabled the collection of high-volume cell morphology data, allowing new molecular embedding models to learn from the experimental phenotypic perturbations of a molecule in a cell. Previously, we developed Molecule-Morphology Contrastive Pretraining (MoCoP), a strategy for aligning small molecule embeddings to morphology fingerprints extracted through CellProfiler. The resulting molecular representation showed transferable performance for quantitative structure--activity relationship (QSAR) prediction tasks. Here, we extend the method by using a deep-learning-based cell image encoding pipeline to extract more feature-rich morphology profiles and align them to the molecular embeddings through contrastive learning. The new embeddings encode more accurate information on how molecules perturb cell morphology and enable improvements for QSAR predictions through either fixed-embedding linear probes or fully flexible fine-tuning. Morphology retrieval performance scales log-linearly with training data size, suggesting continued improvements as larger datasets become available. The improved MoCoP v2 also achieves superior performance on toxicity prediction and competitive results on ADME and activity benchmarks, when compared with existing molecular embedding models that use both cell morphology and transcriptomic data during training.

AI.tldr: MoCoP v2 aligns molecule embeddings with deep-learning-derived cell morphology profiles via contrastive learning, improving QSAR, toxicity, and ADME predictions over prior methods.
AI.motivation: To extract richer cell morphology profiles from images and better capture how molecules perturb cell morphology, enabling more transferable and accurate molecular representations for downstream prediction tasks.
AI.method: Extends MoCoP by replacing CellProfiler features with a deep-learning-based cell image encoding pipeline to extract feature-rich morphology profiles, then aligning them to small molecule embeddings through contrastive learning.
AI.result: New embeddings encode more accurate morphology perturbation information, improving QSAR predictions via fixed-embedding linear probes or full fine-tuning. Morphology retrieval scales log-linearly with training data size, and MoCoP v2 shows superior toxicity prediction and competitive ADME/activity benchmarks versus existing models using morphology and transcriptomic data.
AI.conclusion: Deep-learning image encoding boosts MoCoP's molecular representations, delivering stronger transferable performance and scalability, positioning it as a competitive embedding strategy across diverse molecular prediction tasks.

title: SAGE: A sampling-aware global evaluation benchmark for species distribution modeling
summary: Knowing where species occur is fundamental for biodiversity research and conservation. Species distribution models (SDMs) link species observations to environmental conditions to estimate their spatial distribution. However, accuracy varies with the underlying data and models, making it essential to know for which species models can be trusted. Deep-learning-based SDMs ("DeepSDMs") now jointly model thousands of species, drawing on hundreds of millions of community-science records. At this scale, averaging performance hides substantial species-level variability, particularly for rare species, often of greatest conservation concern. Records are also strongly biased, making occurrence counts misleading. Accounting for these factors is essential for a reliable and informative evaluation of multi-species SDMs. Here, we introduce a Sampling-Aware Global Evaluation (SAGE) benchmark, combining GBIF records for training with sPlotOpen vegetation plots for presence-absence evaluation across 5771 plant species. We propose an evaluation framework that groups species based on two properties, sampling effort and relative prevalence, which describe how densely a species' range is sampled and how frequently the species is recorded. Evaluating single-species SDMs and multi-species DeepSDMs, we find that Random Forests and DeepSDMs perform best overall, but neither dominates: DeepSDMs outperform single-species SDMs for infrequently recorded species while offering no consistent advantage for well-sampled ones. Crucially, this advantage emerges only when established bias-correction practices, such as spatial thinning and reweighting, are carried over to the deep-learning setting. SAGE helps identify the species and data conditions for which a given approach is beneficial, thereby supporting the development of more transparent and ecologically credible SDMs. Data and code: https://earens.github.io/sage/

AI.tldr: SAGE is a sampling-aware benchmark for multi-species species distribution models, using GBIF training records and sPlotOpen presence-absence evaluation across 5771 plant species, revealing species-level performance variability linked to sampling effort and prevalence.
AI.motivation: Species distribution models (SDMs) are fundamental for biodiversity research and conservation, but accuracy varies with data and models. Deep-learning-based SDMs (DeepSDMs) now model thousands of species from hundreds of millions of biased community-science records. At this scale, average performance hides substantial species-level variability, especially for rare species, and record bias makes occurrence counts misleading. A reliable, sampling-aware evaluation is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce SAGE (Sampling-Aware Global Evaluation), combining GBIF records for training with sPlotOpen vegetation plots for presence-absence evaluation across 5771 plant species. They group species by two properties: sampling effort and relative prevalence, describing how densely a species' range is sampled and how frequently it is recorded, then evaluate single-species SDMs and multi-species DeepSDMs.
AI.result: Random Forests and DeepSDMs perform best overall, but neither dominates: DeepSDMs outperform single-species SDMs for infrequently recorded species while offering no consistent advantage for well-sampled ones. This advantage emerges only when bias-correction practices like spatial thinning and reweighting are carried over to the deep-learning setting.
AI.conclusion: SAGE helps identify the species and data conditions under which a given modeling approach is beneficial, supporting more transparent and ecologically credible SDMs. Data and code are available at https://earens.github.io/sage/.

title: Slow-fast dynamics of the McKean model with stochastic resetting and diffusion
summary: In this paper we investigate the combined effects of stochastic resetting and diffusion on a slow--fast dynamical system given by the piecewise-linear McKean model. That is, the fast variable $v$ is subject to Gaussian white noise with effective diffusivity $D$ and is reset to a fixed value $v_r$ at a random sequence of times generated from a Poisson process with rate $r$. Assuming that resetting occurs on the fast timescale, we freeze the slow variable \(w\) under an adiabatic approximation and determine the resulting non-equilibrium stationary state (NESS) of the fast variable as the solution of a modified Fokker--Planck equation. We show that the NESS can be expressed in terms of parabolic cylinder functions, whose asymptotic behavior allows us to recover the corresponding NESS without diffusion in the small-diffusion limit. The NESS is used to derive an averaged equation for the slow dynamics, whose solution converges to a stable fixed point \(w^*\) that depends on \(D\), \(r\) and \(v_r\). This fixed point effectively determines the long-time behaviour of the full system. Finally, we analyze the regime in which resetting occurs on the same timescale as the slow variable. We show how the slow variable now undergoes noisy oscillations due to resetting-induced switching between branches of the fast nullcline and derive the corresponding NESS for $w$ in the non-diffusive case.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the combined effects of stochastic resetting and diffusion on the slow-fast piecewise-linear McKean model. Under an adiabatic approximation, the fast variable's non-equilibrium stationary state (NESS) is derived and expressed via parabolic cylinder functions. The NESS yields an averaged slow dynamics converging to a fixed point w* depending on D, r, and v_r. A second regime where resetting acts on the slow timescale produces noisy oscillations of w.
AI.motivation: Stochastic resetting combined with diffusion in slow-fast (multiscale) dynamical systems is largely unexplored, and understanding how resetting modifies the stationary and long-time behavior of such systems is of interest.
AI.method: The fast variable v of the piecewise-linear McKean model undergoes Gaussian white noise (diffusivity D) and is reset to v_r via a Poisson process (rate r). Assuming fast-timescale resetting, the slow variable w is frozen adiabatically; the fast NESS solves a modified Fokker-Planck equation, expressed via parabolic cylinder functions. This NESS gives an averaged equation for the slow dynamics. A second regime, with resetting on the slow timescale, is analyzed for branching-induced switching.
AI.result: The fast NESS is expressed in terms of parabolic cylinder functions, and its asymptotics recover the non-diffusive NESS in the small-diffusion limit. The averaged slow dynamics converges to a stable fixed point w* that depends on D, r, and v_r and sets the system's long-time behavior. When resetting acts on the slow timescale, w exhibits noisy oscillations from resetting-induced switching between fast nullcline branches, with the corresponding NESS derived in the non-diffusive case.
AI.conclusion: Resetting and diffusion jointly shape the NESS and long-time behavior of the slow-fast McKean model: on fast timescales they yield a D-, r-, and v_r-dependent stable fixed point, while on slow timescales they induce noisy oscillations of the slow variable.

title: FlatClip: A Geometry-Aware Surface-Level Baseline for fMRI Representation Learning
summary: Recent fMRI foundation models differ substantially in the spatial scale at which they represent brain activity. ROI- and connectivity-based models are efficient but coarse, whereas voxel-level models preserve fine-grained spatial structure but require specialized 3D/4D architectures and costly fMRI-specific pretraining. We ask how effectively an image-pretrained encoder can reuse the spatial organization of cortical activity. Motivated by evidence that macroscale brain activity is strongly constrained by brain geometry, we introduce FlatClip, a frozen-encoder surface-level baseline that renders cortical activity as geometry-aware flatmap sequences and reuses a frozen SigLIP2 image encoder with only a lightweight downstream probe. Across resting-state benchmarks, FlatClip serves as a competitive middle-ground representation, outperforming ROI-level baselines on HCP and ADNI tasks while remaining weaker on PPMI and below the strongest voxel-level models overall. On visual-fMRI decoding, restricting the input to visual or NSD-provided task-active cortex improves performance, highlighting the value of task-relevant cortical coverage. Spatial perturbation controls reduce the predictive performance of flatmap features under both retrained and fixed readouts, and anatomy-linked arrangements consistently outperform vertex permutations across three colormaps. Together, these results position surface-level flatmap sequences as a practical middle-ground baseline between ROI and voxel models, and support the utility of anatomy-linked spatial organization for reusing image-pretrained features. Code is available at https://github.com/OneMore1/FlatClip.

AI.tldr: FlatClip is a frozen-encoder surface-level baseline that renders cortical activity as geometry-aware flatmap sequences and reuses a frozen SigLIP2 image encoder with a lightweight probe to bridge ROI-level and voxel-level fMRI models.
AI.motivation: fMRI foundation models vary in spatial scale: ROI/connectivity models are efficient but coarse, while voxel-level models preserve fine structure but need specialized 3D/4D architectures and costly pretraining. The paper asks how well an image-pretrained encoder can reuse the spatial organization of cortical activity, motivated by evidence that macroscale brain activity is constrained by brain geometry.
AI.method: FlatClip renders cortical activity as geometry-aware flatmap sequences and feeds them to a frozen SigLIP2 image encoder, adding only a lightweight downstream probe.
AI.result: Across resting-state benchmarks, FlatClip is a competitive middle-ground representation: it outperforms ROI-level baselines on HCP and ADNI but is weaker on PPMI and below the strongest voxel-level models. On visual-fMRI decoding, restricting input to visual or NSD task-active cortex improves performance. Spatial perturbation controls reduce predictive performance, and anatomy-linked arrangements consistently beat vertex permutations across three colormaps.
AI.conclusion: Surface-level flatmap sequences are a practical middle-ground baseline between ROI and voxel models, supporting the utility of anatomy-linked spatial organization for reusing image-pretrained features. Code is available at https://github.com/OneMore1/FlatClip.

title: Multiphysics Simulation Framework for Continuous Ion Transport and Energetics in Atmospheric Pressure Interfaces
comment: 40 pages, 15 figures including the supporting information
summary: Optimizing atmospheric pressure interfaces requires balancing efficient ion transport with unwanted collision activation. The complex environment at the inlet region, including rapid pressure drops, RF/DC electric fields, ion-gas collisions, and space charge effects, makes simulation of this system challenging. In this work, we introduce MuCITE (Multiphysics simulation for Continuous Ion Transport and Energetics), which combines continuous ion injection, precomputed electric and gas flow fields, and particle-in-cell space charge updates. Furthermore, by employing improved impulsive collision theory, it can not only predict transport but also analyze the loss position of ions and the evolution of their kinetic energy, internal energy, and dissociation probability during transport. Transport predictions with ion currents and activation trends of in-source fragmentation were compared with experimental measurements using a custom-built source and a Q-Exactive HF source. The results show that the simulation predictions agree well with the experimental results and can serve as a reference before experiments. MuCITE allows users to derive ion transport, output beam characteristics, and ion energy through the configurable interface geometry and operating conditions. AI.motivation: Optimizing atmospheric pressure interfaces requires balancing efficient ion transport against unwanted collision activation. The complex inlet environment—rapid pressure drops, RF/DC electric fields, ion-gas collisions, and space charge effects—makes simulating this system challenging.

title: Collective impact of opinion formation on agent-based epidemic dynamics
summary: Epidemic spread and collective opinion formation are tightly coupled processes: individual beliefs about the severity of an outbreak and the value of protective measures shape behavior, while the evolving epidemic itself reshapes public sentiment through risk perception. We propose an agent-based framework that couples opinion dynamics with a compartmental epidemic model, in which each agent carries both a health status and a continuous opinion variable describing adherence to protective measures. Opinion evolution is driven by binary interactions among agents and by an exogenous background field that reflects the current state of the epidemic, while the disease transmission rate depends explicitly on the opinions of interacting agents. Using methods of statistical mechanics, we characterize the resulting macroscopic system for the compartmental mass fractions and mean opinions in both far-from-equilibrium and close-to-equilibrium regimes. The calibration shows that incorporating behavioral opinion dynamics substantially improves the interpretation of epidemic evolution. In particular, the inferred risk perception function evolves consistently with the observed epidemic burden, indicating that behavioral adaptation can explain part of the temporal variation that would otherwise be absorbed into time-dependent transmission parameters. Our results illustrate how integrating opinion heterogeneity in kinetic epidemic models offers quantitative insights into the feedback between behavior and disease spread.

AI.motivation: Epidemic spread and collective opinion formation are tightly coupled: beliefs about outbreak severity and protective measures shape behavior, while the evolving epidemic reshapes public sentiment through risk perception. Existing models often ignore this feedback, absorbing behavioral effects into time-dependent transmission parameters.
AI.method: An agent-based model where each agent has a health status and a continuous opinion variable on adherence to protective measures. Opinion evolution is driven by binary interactions and an exogenous background field reflecting the epidemic state; transmission rate depends explicitly on interacting agents' opinions. Statistical mechanics methods characterize macroscopic compartmental mass fractions and mean opinions in far-from-equilibrium and close-to-equilibrium regimes.
AI.result: Calibration shows incorporating behavioral opinion dynamics substantially improves interpretation of epidemic evolution. The inferred risk perception function evolves consistently with observed epidemic burden, indicating behavioral adaptation explains part of temporal variation otherwise absorbed into time-dependent transmission parameters.
AI.conclusion: Integrating opinion heterogeneity in kinetic epidemic models offers quantitative insights into the feedback between behavior and disease spread.
